ICT Forex Strategy: A Complete Guide to Trade Smarter in 2026
Forex Trading Articles | ITBFX Education Hub
October 26, 2026
Content
Add a header to begin generating the table of contents
The ICT forex strategy is a price-action method that times entries around the price levels where institutional orders are presumed to rest, using a fixed sequence: a liquidity sweep, a shift in market structure, then a return to a marked zone inside a defined trading window. A trade is only taken once every step of that sequence lines up; nothing is traded from a single pattern alone. The ICT forex strategy was developed by Michael J. Huddleston, known publicly as the Inner Circle Trader, and it has since spread through retail trading education far beyond its original audience.
This article guides you through the ICT forex strategy and its core concepts. It’s for a trader who already reads candlesticks and swing highs but has collected ICT vocabulary without a way to put it to work. By the end, you will have the five core ICT concepts defined in plain terms, the full entry sequence written as a checklist, and a worked XAUUSD example that shows the sequence end to end on a historical chart. You’ll also have an honest account of where these setups fail and what that costs an account. The goal is an ICT forex strategy that you can test on a demo chart this week, not another glossary to memorize.
What the ICT Forex Strategy Claims, and What It Replaces?
The ICT trading strategy rests on one working assumption: that price is pulled toward pools of resting orders and that the move toward those pools leaves readable footprints on a chart. ICT forex strategy treats this as a model for reading order flow, not as a proven mechanism, and no public data confirms what any specific institution is doing at any given moment. Where a lagging indicator such as RSI or MACD summarizes past price into a line, the ICT concept reads the raw candles for the same information: it looks at where stops likely sit and how price reacts once it reaches them, instead of waiting for an average to catch up with the move that already happened.
Michael J. Huddleston, trading as the Inner Circle Trader, taught the method through free video lessons aimed at retail traders rather than institutions, which is why the terminology spread quickly through forums, Telegram groups, and YouTube channels long before it reached mainstream technical analysis content.
The ICT Concepts You Need Before You Can Read a Setup
These five ICT concepts mark locations on a chart, not trade signals on their own: a liquidity pool, an order block, a fair value gap, a structure shift, and a premium or discount zone. None triggers an entry by itself; the entry comes only once all of them line up.
Liquidity Pools: Where Stop Orders Collect
A liquidity pool is a cluster of resting stops and pending orders above equal highs or below equal lows, and it matters because that concentration gives price a reason to move toward it. Buy-side liquidity sits above old highs; sell-side liquidity sits below old lows. When a price pushes through one of these levels and then reverses, that move is a liquidity sweep, confirmed only after the reversal has already begun, never in advance.
Order Blocks
An ICT order block is the last opposing candle before a sharp, one-directional displacement move, marked as a zone from the candle’s open to its extreme wick, not a single line. A bullish ICT order block is the last bearish candle before an upward displacement; a bearish order block is the last bullish candle before a downward one. Unlike an ordinary support or resistance level drawn from repeated touches, an order block is tied to one specific displacement event and loses relevance once that event is invalidated.
Fair Value Gaps
A fair value gap (FVG) is a three-candle imbalance where the first candle’s wick does not overlap the third candle’s wick, leaving a visible gap in the middle candle’s range; price is thought to return and rebalance that gap before continuing. It is unrelated to a weekend price gap, which forms between Friday’s close and Sunday’s open because the market is shut; an FVG forms inside one continuous session. A gap is not obliged to fill, and many strong trends leave several behind permanently.
Market Structure Shift and Break of Structure
A break of structure (BOS) is a price closing beyond the most recent swing in the direction of the existing trend, confirming continuation. A market structure shift (MSS) is price closing beyond a swing against the trend, signalling a possible change of control. The two are often confused, yet they describe opposite situations. An MSS only matters here when it follows a liquidity sweep; without one, it is treated as ordinary noise rather than a genuine shift.
Premium and Discount Zones
A dealing range runs from a recent significant swing low to swing high, and its midpoint is the equilibrium, or 50 percent, level; the upper half is premium and the lower half is discount. The rule of thumb favors sell setups in premium and buy setups in discount. This filter can reject an order block that otherwise looks valid, for example, one sitting deep in premium. The 50 percent line is a guide drawn from swing structure, not a precise mechanical boundary.
ICT Kill Zones and the Session Clock
The ICT kill zones are specific windows of the day, stated here in UTC alongside the local time of the exchange they cover, since a session time with no time zone is the most common error in this kind of content. The Asian range is read for bias, not traded directly, since it rarely carries enough volume to confirm a structure shift. These figures are anchored to local exchange hours, so they move twice a year: under the US rule, clocks move forward on the second Sunday of March and back on the first Sunday of November, and under the UK rule, British Summer Time runs from the last Sunday of March to the last Sunday of October. During those summer months, each UTC window above effectively falls one hour earlier. Broker server time is a separate clock again; check the offset on your own platform before marking any window on a live chart.
The Sequence: How the Pieces Form One Setup
ICT trading strategy is a sequence, not a set of patterns: a liquidity sweep, a structure shift, and a return to a marked zone, evaluated in that order, every time.
The order is fixed: a liquidity sweep, then a market structure shift, then a return into the order block left behind, with a fair value gap as an optional confluence, inside a kill zone.
Liquidity sweep.
Price pushes through an equal high or low and reverses; if it keeps running instead of turning, the setup is already void.
Structure shift.
Price closes beyond the swing against the prior trend; without a prior sweep, this step does not count as meaningful.
Return to the order block.
Price pulls back into the last opposing candle before the displacement; no return means no entry.
Confluence check.
A fair value gap inside or near the order block adds weight; its absence does not disqualify the setup alone.
Timing filter.
The return must land inside a kill zone; the same behaviour outside those windows carries less confidence.
This sequence assumes a market with a readable range and a recent liquidity target; a thin, directionless session with no clean equal highs or lows is the condition under which it should not be attempted. Stop logic sits beyond the swept swing; target logic aims at the next opposite liquidity pool, with no specific level implied here.
One Setup From Start to Finish on XAUUSD
What follows is a historical illustration on a past chart, built to show the five-step sequence in order; it is not a trade recommendation and should not be read as a signal for any current position. The chart data referenced is from early 2026, used purely as teaching material.
On the 4-hour chart, XAUUSD swept a cluster of equal highs that had held for two weeks, then closed back below them, marking the liquidity sweep. On the 15-minute chart, used for entry precision, price then closed beyond the most recent higher low, confirming a bearish structure shift. Price pulled back into the bearish order block left before the displacement leg down, overlapping a fair value gap from the same move, with the return landing inside the New York open window.
For the arithmetic, assume the ICT order block sat 12.00 dollars per ounce above the swept high, used as the stop distance, and the next sell-side liquidity pool sat 24.00 dollars below entry, used as the target distance, a 1:2 ratio in this illustration only. Position size is left as a variable, covered next. What would have invalidated this exact setup: a close back above the order block high, meaning the zone failed to hold and the sequence should be abandoned rather than averaged?
When ICT Forex Strategy Setups Fail, and What It Costs You
Yes, the ICT forex strategy setups fail routinely, and the sequence exists to filter candidates rather than to guarantee a correct call on any single trade.
The sweep keeps running.
Price breaks the old high or low and never reverses, continuing as a trend instead of handing back the liquidity.
A higher-timeframe retracement looks like a shift.
The entry-timeframe structure shift can simply be a pullback inside a larger trend above it.
A correctly marked order block sits at the wrong location.
The pattern is valid, but the premium or discount filter should have rejected it.
Hindsight marking.
A zone that looks obvious once the move has already happened was not visible in real time, and old charts can overstate how clean the ICT forex strategy feels.
A setup is not disproven by losing; it is only disproven when the exact condition you wrote down in advance actually occurs.
Consider a fixed 1 percent risk per trade, used only as an educational example: five consecutive losing trades reduce an account by roughly 4.9 percent through compounding, requiring about a 5.2 percent gain to recover; ten consecutive losses bring it down near 9.6 percent, requiring close to 10.6 percent.
Position size follows from the stop distance above: the dollar amount risked, divided by the stop distance in price terms, divided by the value of one unit of the instrument. Skip the setup entirely when the required position size breaches your own risk limit, when the sweep happened outside any kill zone, or when the Asian range bias contradicts the direction of the shift.
Trading leveraged financial instruments carries significant risk. Only trade with capital you can afford to lose. This article is educational and is not investment advice.
Execution Reality: Spread, Slippage and Cost Inside a Kill Zone
Yes, a floating spread widens as liquidity thins around a session open or a data release, and that happens at every real broker, ITBFX included; it is a market mechanism, not a broker trick.
Spread floats with market depth, the volume of resting orders near the current price; when depth drops at a release, the buy-sell gap widens and slippage, a fill away from the requested price, becomes more likely in either direction, including a fill better than requested, known as positive slippage. Measured against the 24.00 dollar target distance from the worked example above, a few tenths of a dollar in spread and commission is a small fraction of the trade, though the same cost against a tighter stop matters more.
On the Gold account, the published spread is raw, from 0 pips, with a commission of 3 USD per lot on the ounce contract, charged once on the deal that opens the position. Commission and account terms do not change during a release, while spread and market depth do. Order execution runs under 85 milliseconds on every account type. To check this independently, compare the spread at three moments: mid-London session, a quiet Asian hour, and the instant of a major release, using an economic calendar to mark the moment.
Named ICT Models: Turtle Soup, Silver Bullet and Optimal Trade Entry
Each named model is the same sweep, shift, entry sequence with one extra filter attached, not a separate system in its own right.
Turtle Soup
adds a false-breakout filter: it looks for a sweep of a well-known swing point that traps breakout traders on the wrong side. It degrades on genuine breakouts, where the sweep simply continues as a real trend move.
Silver Bullet
adds a fixed one-hour timing filter, usually tied to the New York open, looking for the full sequence inside that single hour. It degrades on days with no meaningful liquidity event inside that narrow window.
Optimal Trade Entry
adds a retracement-depth filter, waiting for price to pull back into a specific portion of the prior leg before treating the order block as valid. It degrades when the retracement overshoots that depth and invalidates the leg entirely.
None of these variants is presented here as superior to the base sequence; each simply narrows the conditions under which a trader will act on it.
Strengths and Limitations of the ICT Approach
Whether the ICT trading strategy suits a trader depends on temperament and schedule more than on any inherent superiority over other price-action approaches.
Defined invalidation.
Every step carries a condition that voids the setup, which keeps the method from drifting into pure discretion.
A repeatable checklist.
The same five steps apply across instruments and timeframes once the vocabulary is fixed.
Transfers across markets.
The logic does not depend on one asset, though liquidity behaves differently across instruments.
The honest limitation of the ICT trading strategy is not the chart; it is the discretion every trader brings to marking it.
Set against the strengths above: marking is discretionary, so two traders on the same chart often disagree on exactly where a zone begins and ends. The method is time-of-day dependent, excluding anyone who cannot be at a screen during the kill zone windows. The learning curve is genuinely long, often months before consistency appears. Most importantly, the underlying premise, that price is deliberately driven toward resting liquidity, is a model for reading order flow, not a documented mechanism confirmed by any exchange or regulator, and it stays contested among analysts.
How to Learn and Test ICT Without Risking Capital?
The starting point is a testing sequence, not another reading list.
Mark without trading.
Spend one to two weeks marking sweeps, shifts, and order blocks on past charts with no money involved, until the marking stays consistent day to day.
Forward-test on a demo account.
ITBFX issues a demo account from the client panel or through support for practising a strategy with no real money at risk; log every setup against the five conditions, noting which were present and which were missing.
Move to the smallest real size that feels comfortable
, because a demo account does not reproduce the psychology of trading with real money, and that gap only shows once capital is actually at stake.
Journal fields worth recording: the date and kill zone, which conditions were present, the stop and target distance, the outcome, and a short note on what would have changed the read. Anyone searching for an ICT forex strategy PDF, a book, or a PDF shared through a Telegram group should treat free unofficial material carefully, since much of it strips out the invalidation rules and keeps only what looks impressive in hindsight. The original methodology comes from Michael J. Huddleston’s own public teaching as the Inner Circle Trader, and no fixed ICT forex strategy win rate exists in any published, independently verified dataset.
The Checklist You Can Take to the Chart Tonight
With the sequence, the vocabulary, and one worked example behind you, the decision left is whether to spend the next few weeks testing the ICT forex strategy against your own charts.
Mark the range
on your higher timeframe and note the nearest untouched equal highs or lows.
Wait for a sweep
of one of those levels, confirmed only by a close back through it.
Confirm a structure shift
on your entry timeframe, and discard the setup if no sweep preceded it.
Mark the order block and any fair value gap
left by the displacement that followed the shift.
Check the kill zone and the premium or discount filter
, and write down, in advance, the exact close that would invalidate the setup.
Run this checklist against a demo account first, record every outcome against the five conditions, and let a written record, not a feeling about the last trade, decide whether this method earns a place in your own routine.

Frequently Asked Questions
What is the ICT forex strategy?
The ICT forex strategy is a price-action trading approach developed by Michael J. Huddleston, known as the Inner Circle Trader. It uses concepts such as liquidity sweeps, market structure shifts, order blocks, fair value gaps, and trading-session timing to identify potential entries.
Does the ICT forex strategy work?
The ICT forex strategy can provide a structured way to analyze price action, but its effectiveness is not guaranteed. Results depend on how consistently a trader identifies setups, manages risk, and executes trades. There is no independently verified win rate that applies to all ICT traders, so test the rules on historical charts and a demo account before risking capital.
What are the main concepts of ICT trading?
The five core concepts covered in this guide are liquidity pools, order blocks, fair value gaps, market structure shifts, and premium or discount zones. ICT traders also use kill zones to focus on specific trading-session windows. These concepts help define a setup, but none guarantees a successful trade on its own.
What is the best timeframe for the ICT forex strategy?
There is no single best timeframe for every ICT setup. Some traders use a higher timeframe, such as the 4-hour chart, to identify significant swing levels and a lower timeframe, such as the 15-minute chart, to confirm a structure shift and refine an entry. The best combination is one you can apply consistently and test against historical data.
What is the difference between a liquidity sweep and a break of structure?
A liquidity sweep occurs when price moves beyond a previous high or low where stop orders may collect, then reverses back through the level. A break of structure (BOS) occurs when price closes beyond a relevant swing in the direction of the existing trend, suggesting continuation. A market structure shift (MSS), by contrast, is a break against the prior trend that may signal a change in direction.
What is an ICT fair value gap?
An ICT fair value gap (FVG) is a three-candle price pattern in which the first candle’s wick does not overlap the third candle’s wick, leaving an imbalance around the middle candle. Traders may watch for price to return to this area, but a fair value gap does not have to fill and should not be treated as a standalone entry signal.
Is the ICT forex strategy suitable for beginners?
Beginners can learn the ICT forex strategy, but its terminology and discretionary chart marking can make it challenging. Start by learning one concept at a time, marking historical charts, and recording setups without trading real money. A demo account can help you test whether you can follow the full entry sequence consistently.
Can the ICT strategy be used for gold (XAUUSD)?
Yes. Traders apply ICT concepts to gold (XAUUSD), including liquidity sweeps, structure shifts, order blocks, and fair value gaps. Gold can move sharply around economic releases and major session opens, so spread, slippage, stop distance, and position size all matter. Test the setup on gold-specific historical data rather than assuming that rules perform the same across every market.
Does the ICT forex strategy have a fixed win rate?
No universal, independently verified win rate exists for the ICT forex strategy. Results vary with the exact rules, market, timeframe, trading costs, and execution. Evaluate a clearly defined setup over a meaningful sample of trades and include losses, spread, commission, and slippage in your results.
